statute_title: Conspiracy to Commit Offense or to Defraud United States
penalty_max: 5 years imprisonment
elements: Agreement between two or more persons to commit a federal offense or defraud the United States
Defendant knowingly and voluntarily joined the conspiracy
At least one overt act committed in furtherance of the conspiracy
enhancements: If object offense carries higher penalty, conspiracy may carry same maximum
Sentencing Guidelines consider underlying offense level (USSG § 2X1.1)
Leadership role enhancement (+2 to +4 levels, USSG § 3B1.1)
Obstruction enhancement (+2 levels, USSG § 3C1.1)
notes: Most versatile federal charging tool. Statute of limitations: 5 years. Pinkerton liability allows co-conspirators to be liable for substantive offenses of other members. No overt act required for drug conspiracies under 21 U.S.C. § 846.

penalty_max: 20 years imprisonment; life if predicate involves murder or kidnapping
fine_max: $25,000 per count or twice the proceeds of the offense
elements: Enterprise affecting interstate or foreign commerce
Defendant associated with or employed by the enterprise
Defendant participated in a pattern of racketeering activity
Pattern: at least two predicate acts within 10 years
Relationship and continuity between predicate acts
enhancements: Civil forfeiture of all interests in enterprise
Criminal forfeiture of proceeds and instrumentalities
Civil RICO treble damages available to victims
USSG § 2E1.1 — base offense level is 19 or underlying offense level, whichever is greater
Leadership role enhancements (USSG § 3B1.1)
notes: Predicate acts include mail fraud, wire fraud, extortion, drug trafficking, murder, kidnapping, bribery, and 35+ other offenses. Statute of limitations: 5 years from last predicate act. Both § 1962(c) (participation) and § 1962(d) (conspiracy) commonly charged.

statute_title: Manufacture, Distribution, or Possession with Intent to Distribute Controlled Substances
penalty_max: 40 years (threshold quantities); life (higher quantities or prior felony)
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally manufactured, distributed, dispensed, or possessed with intent to distribute
A controlled substance
The substance is the type and quantity alleged
mandatory_minimum: 5 years for Schedule I/II threshold quantities (e.g., 500g+ cocaine, 28g+ crack, 100g+ heroin, 1kg+ meth mixture); 10 years for higher quantities
enhancements: § 851 prior felony drug conviction doubles mandatory minimum
Death or serious bodily injury results: 20-year mandatory minimum
Distribution to persons under 21: doubles penalties (§ 859)
Distribution near school/playground: doubles penalties (§ 860)
Use of minor in drug operation: additional 1 year consecutive (§ 861)
§ 924(c) firearm enhancement if weapon involved: +5 to 10+ years consecutive
Career offender designation under USSG § 4B1.1
Continuing criminal enterprise (CCE) under § 848: 20 years to life
notes: Drug quantity is an element under Apprendi — must be charged and proven to jury. Safety valve (§ 3553(f)) may allow below-mandatory-minimum sentence for first-time, non-violent offenders who cooperate. Schedule I/II drugs carry the highest penalties.

statute_title: Unlawful Possession of a Firearm by Prohibited Person
penalty_max: 15 years imprisonment (general); mandatory minimums under ACCA
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm or ammunition
The firearm or ammunition was in or affecting interstate commerce
Defendant knew they were a prohibited person at the time of possession
Defendant's prohibited status (felon, domestic violence misdemeanant, drug user, illegal alien, etc.)
mandatory_minimum: 15 years under Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA, 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)) if 3+ prior violent felony or serious drug offense convictions
enhancements: ACCA enhancement: 15-year mandatory minimum for armed career criminals
§ 924(c): additional 5 years consecutive if firearm used/carried in drug crime or crime of violence
§ 924(c) second conviction: 25 years consecutive
USSG § 2K2.1 enhancements for prior convictions, number of firearms, stolen firearms, trafficking
Obliterated serial number: +2 levels (USSG § 2K2.1(b)(4))
notes: Rehaif v. United States (2019) requires proof defendant knew of prohibited status — critical for defense. Prohibitions apply to: convicted felons, fugitives, controlled substance users, mental health adjudicatees, illegal aliens, domestic violence misdemeanants, persons under indictment. Constructive possession is sufficient.

statute_title: Attempt to Evade or Defeat Tax
penalty_max: 5 years imprisonment
elements: Existence of a tax deficiency (unpaid tax)
Willful attempt to evade or defeat the tax
Affirmative act of evasion (beyond mere failure to file)
enhancements: Sophisticated means enhancement (USSG § 2T1.1(b)(2)): +2 levels
Tax loss determines base offense level (USSG § 2T4.1 table)
Role in offense enhancements apply
Money laundering charges commonly added when proceeds concealed
Restitution mandatory for all victims
notes: Distinct from § 7203 (failure to file, misdemeanor) and § 7206 (filing false return). Willfulness requires specific intent to violate a known legal duty. Statute of limitations: 6 years. Civil tax liability and IRS penalties are separate from criminal exposure.

statute_title: Illegal Entry / Reentry of Removed Alien
offense_class: Federal Misdemeanor (§ 1325 first offense) / Federal Felony (§ 1326)
penalty_max: 6 months (§ 1325 first offense); 2 years (§ 1325 second); 2 years (§ 1326 base); 10 years (prior felony removal); 20 years (prior aggravated felony removal)
elements: § 1325: Alien entered or attempted to enter U.S. at unauthorized time or place, or eluded examination by immigration officers, or entered by willful misrepresentation
§ 1326: Alien was previously removed or departed while removal order pending; alien entered, attempted to enter, or was found in U.S. without permission
enhancements: Prior aggravated felony removal: 20-year maximum (§ 1326(b)(2))
Prior felony (3+ years) removal: 10-year maximum (§ 1326(b)(1))
USSG § 2L1.2: base level 8, +4 if prior felony removal, higher levels for aggravated felonies
Fast-track departures available in many districts reducing sentence
Prior § 1326 convictions may be used as aggravating factors
notes: § 1325 was misdemeanor-ized in 2021 DOJ policy but statute unchanged. Collateral consequences include permanent bar to legal status. USSG § 2L1.2 fast-track programs reduce sentences in border districts.

penalty_max: 20 years imprisonment; 30 years if financial institution or federal disaster relief involved
elements: Defendant devised or participated in a scheme to defraud or obtain money/property by false pretenses
Defendant acted with intent to defraud
Defendant used the U.S. mail (or private carrier) in furtherance of the scheme
The mailing was for the purpose of executing or attempting to execute the scheme
enhancements: USSG § 2B1.1: loss amount drives offense level (see loss table)
10+ victims: +2 levels; 50+ victims: +4 levels
Sophisticated means: +2 levels
Vulnerable victim: +2 levels (USSG § 3A1.1)
Often charged with wire fraud, bank fraud, money laundering as a package
Forfeiture of proceeds mandatory
notes: Extremely broad — each mailing is a separate count. No requirement that victim actually be defrauded (attempt sufficient). Private mail carriers (FedEx, UPS) covered. Honest services fraud (§ 1346) is a subset. Statute of limitations: 5 years (10 years for financial institution fraud).

penalty_max: 20 years imprisonment; 30 years if financial institution or federal disaster relief involved
elements: Defendant devised or participated in a scheme to defraud or obtain money/property by false or fraudulent pretenses
Defendant acted with intent to defraud
Defendant used interstate wire communications (phone, email, internet) in furtherance of the scheme
The wire transmission was for the purpose of executing or attempting to execute the scheme
enhancements: USSG § 2B1.1: loss amount drives guideline range
10+ victims: +2 levels; 50+ victims: +4 levels; 250+ victims: +6 levels
Sophisticated means: +2 levels (USSG § 2B1.1(b)(10))
Abuse of position of trust: +2 levels (USSG § 3B1.3)
Often charged alongside mail fraud, bank fraud, money laundering
Healthcare wire fraud under § 1347: up to 10 years (20 if serious bodily injury, life if death results)
notes: Modern workhorse federal fraud statute. Each email, phone call, or wire transmission is a separate count. Honest services wire fraud (§ 1346) covers breach of fiduciary duty. Statute of limitations: 5 years (10 years if financial institution).

penalty_max: 30 years imprisonment
elements: Defendant executed or attempted to execute a scheme to defraud a federally insured financial institution
OR defendant executed a scheme to obtain money, funds, or property under the custody of a financial institution by false or fraudulent pretenses
Defendant acted with intent to defraud
The scheme involved a federally chartered or insured institution
enhancements: USSG § 2B1.1: loss table drives base offense level
Sophisticated means: +2 levels
Mass marketing fraud: +2 levels
Identity theft aggravated: +2 levels (USSG § 2B1.1(b)(11))
Mandatory restitution to financial institutions
Often accompanies money laundering (§ 1956) and aggravated identity theft (§ 1028A)
notes: Covers virtually all federally insured banks, credit unions, and savings associations. Mortgage fraud, check kiting, loan fraud, and credit card fraud schemes all qualify. Statute of limitations: 10 years. No requirement that the institution actually lose money — attempt sufficient.

statute_title: Securities Fraud / Securities Exchange Act Fraud
penalty_max: 20 years imprisonment (§ 1348 Sarbanes-Oxley provision); 25 years for corporate fraud (§ 1350)
elements: In connection with the purchase or sale of securities
Defendant employed a device, scheme, or artifice to defraud, OR made materially false statements or omissions, OR engaged in any act constituting fraud or deceit
Intent to defraud
Use of interstate commerce, mail, or a national securities exchange
enhancements: USSG § 2B1.1: loss amount determines base offense level
Securities offense enhancement: +4 levels (USSG § 2B1.1(b)(20))
Sophisticated means: +2 levels
250+ victims: +6 levels
Obstruction of SEC investigation: +2 levels
Civil SEC disgorgement and penalties are separate from criminal exposure
SEC may also pursue administrative bar from securities industry
notes: Rule 10b-5 (17 C.F.R. § 240.10b-5) is the primary implementing regulation. Insider trading charged under this provision. Statute of limitations: 5 years from offense. Both DOJ (criminal) and SEC (civil) may prosecute — parallel proceedings common.

penalty_max: 20 years imprisonment
fine_max: $500,000 or twice the amount laundered, whichever is greater
elements: Defendant conducted or attempted a financial transaction
The transaction involved the proceeds of specified unlawful activity (SUA)
Defendant knew the property represented proceeds of some unlawful activity

Defendant acted with intent to promote the SUA, OR knew the transaction was designed to conceal the nature, location, source, ownership, or control of the proceeds, OR transaction was designed to evade reporting requirements
enhancements: § 1956(h) conspiracy: same 20-year maximum
§ 1957 (transactions in criminally derived property over $10,000): additional 10 years
USSG § 2S1.1: offense level from underlying offense + 1 level; conviction under § 1956: +2 levels
Sophisticated laundering: +2 levels
Forfeiture of all laundered funds and facilitating property mandatory (§ 982)
Multiple counts: each transaction is a separate offense
notes: Three theories: (1) promotion, (2) concealment, (3) sting. Over 250 predicate 'specified unlawful activities.' § 1957 (spending criminally derived funds) has lower intent requirement. Extraterritorial jurisdiction for international transactions.

statute_title: Felon in Possession of Firearm or Ammunition
penalty_max: 15 years imprisonment; 15-year mandatory minimum under ACCA
elements: Defendant was previously convicted of a crime punishable by imprisonment for more than one year
Defendant knowingly possessed a firearm or ammunition
The firearm or ammunition had previously moved in or affected interstate commerce
Defendant knew of their prior conviction at the time of possession (Rehaif requirement)
mandatory_minimum: 15 years under ACCA (18 U.S.C. § 924(e)) for defendants with 3+ prior violent felony or serious drug offense convictions
enhancements: ACCA: 15-year mandatory minimum for 3+ qualifying prior convictions
§ 924(c): consecutive 5-30 years if firearm used in crime of violence or drug trafficking
USSG § 2K2.1: prior convictions, stolen firearm, number of firearms, trafficking
Career offender (USSG § 4B1.1) if prior violent felony or drug trafficking conviction
notes: Rehaif v. United States, 139 S. Ct. 2191 (2019): government must prove defendant knew of disqualifying status. Constructive and joint possession both cognizable. Expunged state convictions may still qualify under § 922(g).

statute_title: Illegal Firearms Trafficking / Dealing Without License
penalty_max: 5 years (unlicensed dealing); 15 years (firearms trafficking under § 933)
elements: Defendant engaged in the business of dealing firearms
Without a Federal Firearms License (FFL)
OR transferred firearms to prohibited persons (straw purchases, § 932)
OR transported or received firearms with intent to transfer to prohibited persons
Knowledge or willfulness requirement depending on subsection
enhancements: USSG § 2K2.1(b)(5): +4 levels for trafficking 3+ firearms
§ 2K2.1(b)(6): +4 levels if firearm used/intended for another felony
Stolen firearms: +2 levels (§ 2K2.1(b)(4))
§ 933 firearms trafficking (Bipartisan Safer Communities Act 2022): up to 15 years
§ 932 straw purchasing: up to 15 years
Number of firearms directly affects offense level
notes: Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022) added § 932 (straw purchasing) and § 933 (firearms trafficking) as standalone felonies. Ghost guns (unserialized) increasingly charged. ATF Form 4473 false statements: § 922(a)(6), up to 10 years.

statute_title: Certain Activities Relating to Material Involving Sexual Exploitation of Minors
penalty_min: 5 years (possession first offense); 10 years (distribution/receipt first offense)
penalty_max: 20 years (possession); 20 years (distribution/receipt); 40 years (repeat offender)
elements: Defendant knowingly transported, shipped, received, distributed, reproduced, or possessed
Visual depiction
Depicting a minor (under 18) engaged in sexually explicit conduct
Using any means or facility of interstate or foreign commerce, or affecting interstate commerce
Defendant knew the material contained a visual depiction of a minor in sexually explicit conduct
mandatory_minimum: 5 years (possession); 10 years (production under § 2251); 15 years (distribution with prior)
enhancements: § 2252A covers child pornography involving digital/computer content
USSG § 2G2.2: numerous specific offense characteristics
Sadomasochistic or infant images: +4 levels
Distribution for value: +5 levels
Images depicting violence: +4 levels
Pattern of sexual abuse: +5 levels
Use of computer: +2 levels
Sex Offender Registration (SORNA) mandatory — lifetime in many states
notes: § 2252A is the broader provision covering digital content. Production under § 2251 carries mandatory 15-30 year minimums. PROTECT Act (2003) eliminated certain defenses. Affirmative defense available for possessors who promptly reported to law enforcement.

penalty_max: Life imprisonment
elements: Defendant knowingly persuaded, induced, enticed, or coerced
A minor (under 18) to engage in any sexual activity
Using the mail, any facility of interstate or foreign commerce, or any means or facility of interstate commerce
The sexual activity would constitute a criminal offense under federal, state, or local law
enhancements: § 2422(b) attempt: same 10-year mandatory minimum applies
USSG § 2G1.3: prior sex offense conviction, use of computer, vulnerable victim
Use of computer or internet: +2 levels
Unduly influencing minor: +2 levels
Pattern of activity: +5 levels
Sex Offender Registration (SORNA) mandatory
Often charged alongside § 2252 (child pornography) and § 2423 (travel with intent)
notes: § 2422(b) (inducing minor via internet) is the primary online enticement statute. Government need not prove actual minor involved — adult decoy in sting operation sufficient. Travel to commit sexual act with minor charged under § 2423.

penalty_max: Life imprisonment (large quantities or death results)
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally distributed, dispensed, or possessed with intent to distribute
A controlled substance
Quantity meets or exceeds the threshold for enhanced penalties
Type of controlled substance as alleged
mandatory_minimum: 5 years for Schedule I/II threshold quantities; 10 years for high-quantity thresholds (e.g., 5kg+ cocaine, 280g+ crack, 1kg+ heroin, 5g+ pure meth, 1000kg+ marijuana)
enhancements: Prior felony drug conviction (§ 851 notice): doubles mandatory minimums
Two or more prior felony drug convictions: mandatory life
Death or serious bodily injury results: 20-year mandatory minimum
Drug kingpin (§ 848 CCE): 20 years to life, $4M fine
§ 924(c) firearm: consecutive 5-10 years
School zone (§ 860): doubles penalties
Importation: additional penalties under § 952
Leader/organizer: +4 levels (USSG § 3B1.1)
notes: Drug type and quantity are elements under Apprendi/Alleyne — must be submitted to jury and proven beyond reasonable doubt. Safety valve (USSG § 5C1.2) available only for first-time, nonviolent offenders with limited criminal history who cooperate. Fentanyl enhancements significantly increased post-2018.

penalty_max: 1 year (first offense misdemeanor); 2 years (if prior drug offense); up to 3 years for cocaine base
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed
A controlled substance
Without a valid prescription or legal authorization
enhancements: Prior drug conviction: elevated to felony with 2-year maximum
Two+ prior drug convictions: 3-year maximum
Special cocaine base provision: up to 3 years regardless of prior history
USSG § 2D2.1: base level 4-8 depending on substance
Deferred prosecution/diversion available for first offenders (§ 844(b))
notes: First Offense Act (§ 3607) allows probation and expungement for first offenders. Federal simple possession charges are relatively rare — most federal drug cases involve trafficking. The FIRST STEP Act (2018) reduced sentencing disparities for crack cocaine.

penalty_max: Life imprisonment for large quantities
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally manufactured
A controlled substance
The type and quantity alleged in the indictment
mandatory_minimum: Same as distribution: 5 years for threshold quantities under § 841(b)(1)(A) and (B)
enhancements: Methamphetamine lab: chemical disposal costs recoverable
Endangering human life while manufacturing: additional 10 years (§ 858)
Manufacturing near schools or playgrounds: doubles penalties (§ 860)
§ 924(c) if firearm present at manufacturing site
Precursor chemical offenses under §§ 841(c), 843
notes: Manufacture, distribute, and possess-with-intent all charge under § 841(a)(1) — penalties identical. Precursor chemical tracking under Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act (2005). 'Manufacturing' includes producing, preparing, propagating, and processing.

statute_title: Possession with Intent to Distribute Controlled Substance
penalty_max: Life imprisonment for large quantities or repeat offenders
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed
A controlled substance
With intent to distribute it
Type and quantity of substance as alleged
mandatory_minimum: Same mandatory minimums as distribution: 5-10 years depending on drug type and quantity
enhancements: § 851 prior conviction notice doubles mandatory minimum
§ 924(c) if firearm present: consecutive 5-10 years
Drug quantity above thresholds triggers § 841(b)(1)(A) or (B) enhancements
Multiple packaging consistent with distribution: circumstantial evidence of intent
Scales, cutting agents, large cash: used to prove intent
Safety valve: available for qualifying first offenders
notes: Intent to distribute proven circumstantially through quantity, packaging, scales, ledgers, communications, and cash. Constructive possession sufficient. Drug type and quantity must be charged in indictment and proven to jury under Apprendi. Often charged alongside § 846 conspiracy.

penalty_min: 20 years if victim under 18 and not parent
penalty_max: Life imprisonment; death if victim dies
elements: Defendant unlawfully seized, confined, inveigled, decoyed, kidnapped, abducted, or carried away
Another person
Held for ransom, reward, or otherwise
Using interstate or foreign commerce, or the victim was transported across state lines or international borders, OR defendant is a federal employee/official, OR victim is a federal employee/official
mandatory_minimum: 20 years if victim is under 18 and perpetrator is not the parent
enhancements: Death results: life imprisonment or death penalty
Victim under 18: 20-year mandatory minimum
Sexual abuse of victim during kidnapping: additional charges and enhancements
Use of firearm: § 924(c) consecutive term
USSG § 2A4.1: starts at level 32 with numerous specific offense characteristics
notes: Federal jurisdiction triggered by interstate transportation OR 24-hour presumption (Lindbergh Law). Parental kidnapping is a separate offense under § 1204. Hostage taking (§ 1203) and carjacking (§ 2119) are related charges. FBI has primary jurisdiction.

penalty_min: 5 years (§ 844(f)); 7 years minimum for § 844(h) (using fire in violent crime)
penalty_max: 20 years; 40 years if serious bodily injury; life if death results
elements: § 844(f): Maliciously damaged or destroyed by fire or explosive any building or property owned/possessed/used by the U.S. government or a federally-funded organization

§ 844(i): Maliciously damaged or destroyed, or attempted to damage or destroy, by means of fire or explosives, any building or property used in interstate commerce or in activity affecting interstate commerce
Defendant acted with malice (intentionally or recklessly)
mandatory_minimum: 5 years (§ 844(f) government property); 7 years consecutive (§ 844(h) use of fire to commit felony)
enhancements: § 844(h): using fire or explosive to commit any federal felony: additional 10 years consecutive
Serious bodily injury results: 7-40 years
Death results: 20 years to life
§ 844(o): civil rights arson (church burning): enhanced penalties
USSG § 2K1.4: base level varies 2-24 based on circumstances
notes: § 844(i) has broad interstate commerce nexus — virtually any commercial building qualifies (Russell v. United States). § 844(h) consecutive term for using fire/explosive to commit another federal felony creates powerful prosecutorial leverage. State arson charges often run parallel.

statute_title: Interference with Commerce by Robbery (Hobbs Act Robbery)
penalty_max: 20 years imprisonment
elements: Defendant obstructed, delayed, or affected commerce
By robbery or extortion, or attempted or conspired to do so
Robbery: unlawful taking or obtaining of property from person or presence of another by actual or threatened force, violence, or fear of injury
The robbery had at least a de minimis effect on interstate commerce
enhancements: § 924(c): 7 years consecutive if firearm brandished; 10 years if discharged
§ 924(c) second count: mandatory 25 years consecutive
USSG § 2B3.1: robbery base level 20 with numerous enhancements
Injury to victim: +2 to +6 levels
Carjacking (§ 2119): 15-25 years minimum if death results
Bank robbery (§ 2113): separate statute, up to 20 years
notes: De minimis commerce nexus required — courts have found nexus from a single convenience store robbery. Hobbs Act extortion and robbery are distinct theories under § 1951. § 924(c) stacking with Hobbs Act robberies is a major sentencing driver.

penalty_min: 2 years consecutive (general offenses); 5 years consecutive (terrorism-related offenses)
penalty_max: 2 years consecutive (added to underlying offense); 5 years consecutive for terrorism
elements: Defendant knowingly transferred, possessed, or used
Without lawful authority
A means of identification of another person
During and in relation to a predicate felony enumerated in § 1028A(c)
mandatory_minimum: 2 years consecutive to any other term of imprisonment
enhancements: Sentence CANNOT run concurrently — always 2 years consecutive (Flores-Figueroa v. United States, 2009)
Multiple counts: each use of different victims' identity is a separate count
§ 1028 (identity document fraud): up to 15 years for underlying identity document crime
USSG § 2B1.6: offense level = level from underlying predicate offense
Terrorism-related: 5 years consecutive
notes: Flores-Figueroa v. United States (2009): government must prove defendant knew the means of identification belonged to a real, actual person. § 1028A(c) lists over 50 predicate offenses. Restitution to victims mandatory. Distinct from § 1028 (fraud related to identity documents).

statute_title: Counterfeiting Obligations or Securities of the United States
penalty_max: 20 years imprisonment
elements: Defendant falsely made, forged, counterfeited, or altered
Any obligation or other security of the United States
With intent to defraud
enhancements: § 472: passing/uttering counterfeit obligations: up to 20 years
§ 473: dealing in counterfeit obligations: up to 20 years
§ 474: plates/stones used for counterfeiting: up to 25 years
USSG § 2B5.1: counterfeit value determines offense level
Secret Service has primary investigative jurisdiction
notes: Covers currency, bonds, Treasury securities, postage stamps, and other government obligations. § 510 covers counterfeit U.S. government checks. Counterfeit access devices (credit cards): § 1029. Secret Service and Treasury have primary jurisdiction.

statute_title: Influencing or Injuring Officer or Juror Generally (Obstruction of Justice)
penalty_max: 10 years imprisonment; life if obstruction related to murder or attempted murder
elements: There was a pending federal judicial proceeding
Defendant knew of the proceeding
Defendant corruptly endeavored to influence, obstruct, or impede the due administration of justice
enhancements: § 1512 (tampering with witnesses): up to 30 years if involving killing/attempted killing
§ 1519 (destruction of records): up to 20 years — covers document shredding during investigation
§ 1001 (false statements to federal agents): up to 5 years
USSG § 3C1.1: +2 levels for obstruction of this case being sentenced
§ 1512(c)(2): broader corrupt obstruction provision
Martha Stewart rule: lying to federal investigators is a separate federal crime under § 1001
notes: Omnibus clause of § 1503 broadly covers corrupt influence of any judicial proceeding. § 1519 (Sarbanes-Oxley) covers document destruction even before formal proceedings begin. Each obstructive act can be a separate count.

penalty_max: Revocation: Class A felony: up to 5 years; Class B: up to 3 years; Class C/D: up to 2 years; Class E/misdemeanor: up to 1 year
elements: Defendant was serving a term of supervised release
Defendant violated a condition of supervised release
Violation proven by preponderance of the evidence (not beyond reasonable doubt)
Court determines appropriate response: modification, continued supervision, or revocation
enhancements: Mandatory revocation for: possession of controlled substance, possession of dangerous weapon, new felony conviction
Grade A violation (new felony with 1+ year sentence): revocation mandatory
Grade B violation (other new felony or high-level misdemeanor): court discretion
Grade C violation (low-level misdemeanor or technical): modification usually preferred
Prior revocations: USSG Chapter 7 increases revocation sentence
New federal crime during supervision: prosecution for new offense PLUS revocation
notes: Supervised release imposed at sentencing under § 3583(a) — mandatory for felonies. Violation hearings under Fed. R. Crim. P. 32.1 — lower burden than trial. USSG Chapter 7 provides policy statements (not binding guidelines). Modification, termination, or revocation are all options.

offense_class: Federal (summary or criminal contempt — no fixed offense class)
penalty_max: No statutory maximum for criminal contempt (judge's discretion); 6 months for petty contempt
elements: A lawful court order existed
Defendant had knowledge of the order
Defendant willfully violated or disobeyed the order, or misbehaved in presence of court, or disobeyed process
enhancements: Civil contempt: coercive (continues until compliance) — different from criminal contempt
Criminal contempt: punitive (fixed punishment for past violation)
Summary contempt (§ 401(1)): immediate for in-court behavior
Indirect contempt requires notice and hearing (Fed. R. Crim. P. 42)
Jury trial right for sentences of 6+ months
notes: § 401 governs criminal contempt of federal court. Civil contempt is not § 401 — it is coercive via court's equitable power. Failure to comply with grand jury subpoena charged as contempt. § 401 sentences run independently from other criminal sentences.

statute_title: Prohibited Acts — National Firearms Act (NFA) Violations
penalty_max: 10 years imprisonment
elements: Defendant possessed, transferred, or made
A firearm as defined under the National Firearms Act (machine gun, silencer/suppressor, short-barreled rifle/shotgun, destructive device, 'any other weapon')
Without proper NFA registration or in violation of NFA tax requirements
The NFA requires a $200 tax, registration, and ATF approval for all NFA items
enhancements: § 924(c): additional consecutive sentence if NFA weapon used in crime of violence or drug trafficking
USSG § 2K2.1: higher base offense level for NFA weapons (level 18 for silencer/machine gun)
Machine gun conversion: automatic weapon conversion device carries same penalties
§ 922(o): separate prohibition on machine gun transfers/possession
Criminal forfeiture of any property used to facilitate offense
notes: NFA (26 U.S.C. § 5801 et seq.) regulates machine guns, suppressors, short-barreled rifles (barrel under 16 inches), short-barreled shotguns (barrel under 18 inches), destructive devices, and 'any other weapons.' Garland v. Cargill (2024): bump stocks are NOT machine guns. Glock auto switches (machine gun conversion devices) are a major enforcement priority.

penalty_max: 10 years; 20 years if serious bodily injury results; life or death penalty if death results
elements: Defendant knowingly and willfully executed or attempted to execute a scheme or artifice
To defraud any healthcare benefit program
OR to obtain money or property from a healthcare benefit program by false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises
In connection with the delivery of or payment for healthcare benefits, items, or services
enhancements: Anti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b): up to 10 years for kickbacks for Medicare/Medicaid referrals
False Claims Act civil liability: treble damages plus $15,000+ per claim
USSG § 2B1.1: loss amount drives offense level
OIG mandatory exclusion from federal healthcare programs
Often charged alongside wire fraud (§ 1343) and money laundering (§ 1956)
notes: False billing, upcoding, unbundling, phantom billing, kickbacks for referrals, and unnecessary procedures all qualify. HHS-OIG/FBI/DOJ Medicare Fraud Strike Force actively prosecutes.

penalty_max: 5 years imprisonment (general); 8 years if related to terrorism or sex offense
elements: Defendant made a false statement, representation, or certification
OR concealed or covered up a material fact
In a matter within the jurisdiction of any branch of the U.S. government
The statement was material (capable of influencing the government's action)
Defendant acted knowingly and willfully
enhancements: Terrorism connection: 8-year maximum
Often charged alongside conspiracy (§ 371) for making false statements in furtherance of scheme
USSG § 3C1.1 obstruction enhancement may apply to underlying offense
Each individual false statement may be charged as a separate count
notes: Brogan v. United States (1998): no 'exculpatory no' doctrine — simple denial to federal agent is a federal crime. No requirement that government be actually deceived. Covers false statements to any agency (FBI, IRS, DHS, EPA, etc.). Famous use: Martha Stewart, Michael Flynn, Roger Stone prosecutions.

penalty_max: 5 years imprisonment
elements: Defendant took an oath to testify truthfully before a competent tribunal or officer
Defendant willfully stated as true something they believed to be false
The false statement was material to the proceeding
enhancements: § 1623 (false declarations before grand jury/court): same penalty, but two-witness rule does not apply
§ 1622 (subornation of perjury): inducing another to commit perjury: same 5-year maximum
Often charged alongside obstruction of justice (§ 1503) and false statements (§ 1001)
USSG § 2J1.3: base level 14 for perjury
Recantation defense: § 1623(d) — false statement retracted before it substantially affects the proceeding
notes: Two-witness rule under § 1621: the falsity must be proven by two witnesses or one witness plus corroborating evidence. § 1623 eliminates the two-witness rule. Materiality is an element under United States v. Gaudin (1995) — must go to jury.

penalty_max: 15 years imprisonment (bribery); 2 years (illegal gratuity)
fine_max: Three times the monetary equivalent of the thing of value / $250,000
elements: § 201(b) Bribery: Defendant directly or indirectly gave, offered, or promised a thing of value
To a public official (or one selected to be an official)
With intent to influence an official act, cause the official to act contrary to duty, or induce the official to commit fraud on the United States
§ 201(c) Illegal Gratuity: Thing of value given for or because of official act (no quid pro quo required)
enhancements: USSG § 2C1.1: offense level 12 base; numerous enhancements for value of bribes, role
More than one bribe: +2 levels
High-level official: +4 levels
Honest services fraud (§ 1346) commonly charged alongside § 201
Hobbs Act extortion (§ 1951) for extortion under color of official right
Forfeiture of bribe proceeds mandatory
notes: McDonnell v. United States (2016) narrowed 'official act' — must be formal exercise of official power, not mere meetings or calls. Federal program bribery under § 666 covers recipients of $10K+ in federal funds. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (15 U.S.C. § 78dd-1) covers bribing foreign officials.

penalty_max: 2 years (§ 875 threatening communications); 20 years (Hobbs Act § 1951)
elements: § 875: Defendant transmitted in interstate commerce a communication containing a threat to kidnap, injure, or demand ransom, with intent to extort money or valuable consideration
§ 1951 (Hobbs Act): Defendant induced victim to part with property
Using actual or threatened force, violence, fear of injury, OR under color of official right
Affecting interstate commerce
enhancements: § 879: threatening the President/Vice President: up to 5 years
Hobbs Act conspiracy (§ 1951(a)): same 20-year maximum
USSG § 2B3.2: base level 18 for extortion; numerous victim harm enhancements
§ 924(c) if firearm involved in Hobbs Act
Often charged with wire fraud when electronic communications used
notes: Hobbs Act extortion under color of official right is the primary mechanism for prosecuting public corruption involving payment demands. § 875 targets threatening communications including email and social media.

penalty_max: 1 year (simple unauthorized access misdemeanor); 5 years (first felony offense); 10 years (second offense); 20 years if reckless damage; life if death results
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly accessed a protected computer
Without authorization OR exceeding authorized access
With intent to defraud, obtain information, cause damage, or extort (depending on subsection charged)
Protected computer: any computer used in interstate commerce, connected to internet, or used by U.S. government/financial institution
enhancements: National security or government computers: enhanced penalties
Financial damage exceeding $5,000 triggers felony threshold
Conspiracy under § 1030(b): same penalties as underlying offense
USSG § 2B1.1 or § 2M3.2 depending on computer type accessed
Civil cause of action under § 1030(g) for victims
notes: Van Buren v. United States (2021) narrowly construed 'exceeds authorized access.' § 1030(a)(2) (obtaining information), § 1030(a)(4) (fraud), § 1030(a)(5) (damage) are most common. Ransomware attacks prosecuted under § 1030.

statute_title: Sex Trafficking of Children or by Force, Fraud, or Coercion
penalty_min: 10 years; 15 years if victim 14-17; mandatory life if victim under 14
penalty_max: Life imprisonment
elements: Defendant knowingly recruited, enticed, harbored, transported, provided, obtained, advertised, maintained, patronized, or solicited
Another person
Knowing or in reckless disregard of the fact that the person would be caused to engage in a commercial sex act
By force, fraud, or coercion, OR victim was under 18 years of age
enhancements: § 1589 (forced labor trafficking): up to 20 years; life if death or kidnapping occurs
§ 1592 (document servitude): up to 5 years
TVPA civil cause of action for victims (§ 1595)
Restitution mandatory to all victims
SORNA sex offender registration for sex trafficking convictions
USSG § 2G1.1: offense level 34 base for sex trafficking
notes: Trafficking Victims Protection Act (TVPA). Strict liability as to victim's age if victim is under 18. FOSTA-SESTA (2018) added § 2421A prohibiting internet promotion of prostitution.

penalty_max: 15 years; 25 years if serious bodily injury; life or death if death results or kidnapping occurs
elements: Defendant took a motor vehicle
From the person or presence of another person
By force and violence or by intimidation
With intent to cause death or serious bodily harm
The motor vehicle had been transported, shipped, or received in interstate commerce
enhancements: § 924(c) firearm: additional 7 years consecutive if firearm brandished
§ 924(c): 10 years consecutive if firearm discharged
Serious bodily injury to victim: up to 25 years
Death or kidnapping: life or death penalty
USSG § 2B3.1: base level 20 with carjacking-specific enhancements
Injury enhancements: +1 to +6 levels depending on severity
notes: Federal jurisdiction requires the vehicle to have moved in interstate commerce (virtually all modern vehicles qualify). Holloway v. United States (1999): conditional intent to use force if victim resists satisfies the intent element. Often charged alongside § 924(c) for armed carjacking.

statute_title: Attempt and Conspiracy to Distribute Controlled Substances
penalty_max: Same maximum as underlying completed offense under § 841
elements: Agreement between two or more persons to violate federal drug laws
Defendant knowingly and voluntarily joined the conspiracy
NOTE: No overt act required for drug conspiracies (unlike general conspiracy under § 371)
mandatory_minimum: Same mandatory minimums as substantive offense (5-10 years for threshold quantities)
enhancements: § 851 prior drug conviction: doubles mandatory minimums
Same enhancements as § 841(b) apply based on drug type and quantity
Leader/organizer of conspiracy: +4 levels
Pinkerton liability: co-conspirators liable for foreseeable acts of other members
Safety valve: available for qualifying first-time offenders
Continuing criminal enterprise (§ 848): 20 years to life if supervisor of 5+ persons
notes: Unlike § 371 (general conspiracy), § 846 does not require an overt act — the agreement itself is the crime. Drug quantity attributed based on reasonably foreseeable quantities handled by entire conspiracy (USSG § 1B1.3). Withdrawal defense: must take affirmative steps to withdraw and communicate to co-conspirators before arrest.

statute_title: Clean Water Act / RCRA Criminal Violations
penalty_max: 3-6 years (negligent violations); 3-15 years (knowing violations); 15-35 years (knowing endangerment)
fine_max: $10,000 to $50,000 per day of violation; $250,000 individual / $1,000,000 organization
elements: Defendant discharged pollutants into waters of the U.S. (CWA) OR disposed of hazardous waste (RCRA)
Without a permit or in violation of a permit
Negligently, knowingly, or with knowing endangerment
The substance qualifies as a pollutant or regulated hazardous waste
enhancements: Knowing endangerment: highest tier, up to 15 years under CWA
Second offense: doubled penalties
False statements in permit applications: § 1001 charges
Civil EPA penalties run parallel to criminal prosecution
Responsible corporate officer doctrine: executives personally liable without direct knowledge
USSG § 2Q1.2 (hazardous waste) and § 2Q1.3 (environmental permitting)
notes: Responsible Corporate Officer (RCO) doctrine (United States v. Park, 1975): executives can be convicted without proof of direct involvement if they had authority to prevent violations. Clean Air Act (42 U.S.C. § 7413) and CERCLA have parallel criminal provisions.

statute_title: Theft or Bribery Concerning Programs Receiving Federal Funds
penalty_max: 10 years imprisonment
elements: Agent of an organization or state/local government receiving more than $10,000 in federal benefits in a one-year period
Defendant embezzled, stole, or obtained by fraud $5,000 or more in property
OR defendant intentionally misapplied $5,000 or more of funds of the organization
OR defendant corruptly solicited/accepted something of value intending to be influenced in connection with a transaction worth $5,000 or more
enhancements: Often charged alongside honest services fraud (§ 1346 / §§ 1341/1343)
§ 201 federal bribery charges may be added if federal official
USSG § 2C1.1: offense level based on value of bribes/misappropriated funds
Fiduciary/position of trust enhancement: +2 levels
Forfeiture of proceeds
notes: Extremely broad — covers virtually all state and local government officials due to federal grant funding. Salinas v. United States (1997): § 666 does not require proof of connection between bribe and federal funds. Often paired with honest services wire/mail fraud in public corruption cases.

statute_title: Mortgage Fraud / False Statements to Financial Institution
penalty_max: 30 years (§ 1344 bank fraud); 30 years (§ 1014 false statements to FDIC-insured institution)
elements: § 1014: Defendant knowingly made a false statement or report for the purpose of influencing the action of any federally insured financial institution
In connection with a loan, credit, or other extension of credit
§ 1344: Defendant executed or attempted to execute a scheme to defraud or obtain money from a federally insured financial institution under false pretenses
enhancements: Often charged in conjunction with wire fraud (§ 1343) and mail fraud (§ 1341)
Aggravated identity theft (§ 1028A): additional 2 years consecutive
Money laundering (§ 1956) charges if proceeds concealed
USSG § 2B1.1: loss amount drives offense level
Financial industry insider: potential abuse of trust enhancement
notes: FBI and HUD-OIG have primary jurisdiction. Mortgage fraud includes straw buyer schemes, appraisal fraud, loan application fraud, property flipping with inflated appraisals, and builder bailout schemes. 10-year statute of limitations. Restitution to lenders mandatory.

statute_title: Embezzlement of Government Funds / Theft of Federal Property
penalty_max: 10 years (§ 666 federal program funds); 10 years (§ 641 property over $1,000); 1 year (§ 641 property under $1,000)
elements: § 641: Defendant embezzled, stole, purloined, or knowingly converted to their use
Money, property, or records belonging to the United States or any U.S. agency
OR received, concealed, or retained such property knowing it to be stolen
Value of property determines felony/misdemeanor classification
enhancements: § 666: federal program funds over $5,000 in organizations receiving $10,000+ federal funds
Position of trust: +2 levels (USSG § 3B1.3)
Amount stolen drives offense level under USSG § 2B1.1
Restitution mandatory
Often charged alongside money laundering when proceeds laundered
notes: § 641 covers theft of any federal government property. § 666 covers embezzlement from any organization receiving federal funding (states, cities, universities, nonprofits). Bank employee embezzlement: § 656 (up to 30 years for federally insured institution).

statute_title: Tampering with a Witness, Victim, or Informant
penalty_max: 30 years (if killing or attempting to kill witness); 20 years (if using force/threats); 10 years (if harassing or intimidating); 3 years (corrupt persuasion)
elements: Defendant knowingly used intimidation, threats, corrupt persuasion, or misleading conduct
Toward another person
With intent to influence, delay, or prevent the testimony of the person in an official proceeding
OR with intent to cause the person to withhold testimony, records, or documents
enhancements: § 1512(a): killing or attempting to kill to prevent testimony: up to 30 years
§ 1512(b): threats and corrupt persuasion: up to 20 years
§ 1512(c)(2): corrupt obstruction of official proceeding (broad): up to 20 years
§ 1513 (retaliating against witness): additional charges, up to 30 years if killing
USSG § 3C1.1: +2 levels for obstruction in current case
No requirement that official proceeding be pending — 'contemplated' proceedings covered
notes: § 1512(c)(2) was used in January 6 prosecutions. United States v. Fischer (2024) narrowed § 1512(c)(2) to require evidence impairment. § 1512 has no pending proceeding requirement — covers actions taken before any formal proceeding begins.

penalty_min: 5 years for threshold quantities; 10 years for higher quantities
penalty_max: Life imprisonment for large quantities
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally imported or exported
A controlled substance
Into or out of the United States
Without legal authorization
Drug type and quantity as alleged
mandatory_minimum: Same tiered structure as § 841(b): 5 years for threshold quantities, 10 years for higher quantities
enhancements: § 851 prior drug conviction doubles mandatory minimum
Death or serious bodily injury: 20-year mandatory minimum
§ 963 conspiracy to import/export: same penalties as underlying offense
Organizational leaders: +4 levels
§ 960a: drug offenses benefiting terrorist organizations: 20 years to life
notes: DEA and CBP have joint jurisdiction. § 963 drug importation conspiracy does not require an overt act. Fentanyl importation is a top enforcement priority. Constructive importation when defendant knew contraband was in shipment they controlled.

penalty_max: 20 years imprisonment
fine_max: $500,000 or twice the amount laundered, whichever is greater
elements: Agreement between two or more persons to commit money laundering under §§ 1956 or 1957
Defendant knowingly and intentionally joined the conspiracy
NOTE: No overt act required for § 1956(h) money laundering conspiracy
enhancements: No overt act required — the agreement itself constitutes the offense
USSG § 2S1.1: same as substantive money laundering; +2 levels for § 1956 conviction
Underlying specified unlawful activity drives base offense level
Forfeiture of all funds involved in the conspiracy
Often charged with underlying predicate crimes (drug trafficking, fraud, etc.)
notes: § 1956(h) conspiracy does not require an overt act — broader than § 371 conspiracy. Enormously powerful because it sweeps in financial institutions and their employees. Kingpin-style prosecutions routinely add § 1956(h) alongside § 846 drug conspiracy. Statute of limitations: 5 years.

penalty_max: Varies by statute
elements: Varies by specific charge
Must be a federal crime with a federal nexus (interstate commerce, federal property, federal official, etc.)
enhancements: Varies by specific offense
U.S. Sentencing Guidelines apply to all federal felony and Class A misdemeanor offenses
Recidivism enhancements under USSG Chapter 4
Role in offense adjustments under USSG Chapter 3B
notes: Catch-all category for federal offenses not listed above. Common examples: Title 18 civil rights violations (§ 241, § 242), Espionage Act (§ 793), Foreign Agents Registration Act (§ 612), election interference offenses (§ 594-611), food and drug misbranding (21 U.S.C. § 333), bankruptcy fraud (§ 157), market manipulation. Consult federal statutory index for specific statutes.
